title: Looking for AI tools to help bridge the gap between "Idea" and "Fun Core Loop"?
author: wacomlover
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m starting to work on a new 2D arcade project, and I’m hitting a wall that I always struggle with: translating a raw concept into a loop that actually feels *fun*. It’s not the technical side (coding) that slows me down, but the design logic—level scaling, risk/reward placement, and pacing.

Are there any AI services or specific LLM workflows you’ve used to help "unfold" an idea into a playable prototype? Specifically, I’m looking for help with:

* **Level Scaling:** Determining optimal dimensions and layout density.
* **Blueprint Generation:** Visualizing level layouts that create interesting risk/reward scenarios.
* **Progression Systems:** Balancing stats (damage scaling, skill unlocks) so the power curve feels right.

Does anyone have experience using AI as a sounding board for these specific design hurdles?

replies.author: HealthyWest6482
replies.body:
three things I've picked up on with the managing the 'idea factory that constantly haunts us'.

1.) If it's something I'm building for myself, it's more likely to be fun (for me).

2.) If it solves some kind of useful purpose for others (doesn't have to be fun).

3.) If it bridges the gap between what people 'have now' and what they've always wanted.

if you hit 2 of 3, it's in pretty good shape. im talking to codex too much im out here validating my own brain

replies.author: BenTheSodaman
replies.body:
Wholeheartedly agree.

\#1 has been dangerous for me, because as the foundation came together, I enjoyed the play tests a little too much even with a mountain of things to implement, tweak, and polish remaining.

\#3 I see a lot with folks wanting mods, remasters, remakes, demakes, or a concept/theme applied in a different setting. Though several of those being IP issues and risks. Some being knowledge, time, and interest/motivation. etc.

(And #2 I acknowledge, but haven't given it as much thought to sit down and take a shot at it for even myself.)

replies.author: Substantial_Law1451
replies.body:
I've been using codex with access to the files and building in Godot, so far it's been smooth. But I'm not interested in doing anything at a professional level, just as a hobby. 


For your specific instance, it'll probably work well because there is a lot of precedence/best practises for the things you listed.


Level scaling is more about ensuring that everything is designed in a modular fashion that makes rapid development and adjustment easy. Sizing, origin positioning, reusability of assets (a wall piece into a long wall into a room as a very light example)


This will make blueprint generation much easier


Powerscaling is naturally all relative so you need a baseline to work up from. The weakest ability upwards - i.e. an auto-attack does 10 dmg so a crit does 20. This again can is a decent application as a starting point because there's a lot of pre existing maffs that can be used to create relative curves.


AI generally struggles with the holistic view of the product as a whole. So in my experience the smaller, simpler the change the better if you're using it for implementation (but you said you didn't have a problem with that so idk)


Ultimately the process is the same as all development. Create, test, adjust, create. The best thing AI can do to help you with actually figuring out what works and doesn't, what's fun and isn't, is finding and facilitating opportunities for really rapid testing and iteration. But as you've noticed, only you can ultimately determine what's fun and what isn't.

replies.author: SplinterOfChaos
replies.body:
Fun is also individual. What's fun to you might not be fun to another. My guiding light is

*"It’s not the job of the artist to give the audience what the audience wants. If the audience knew what they needed, then they wouldn’t be the audience. They would be the artists. It is the job of artists to give the audience what they need.”*

I don't like the phrase "finding the fun" because as the designer, it's actually your job to *define* fun and demonstrate it to the player. To me, this is the difference between thinking like a player and thinking like an artist,.

comments.author: DatabaseConstant7870
comments.body: Okay so if you are vibecoding everything go to gpt and ask it to help you create a master prompt that you can copy and paste in your coding agent and make sure you explain it’s an addition to an existing project and to not change anything that’s already implemented. It will come up with a prompt you should be able to use to get a clean result. You can go into more depth about what’s working and what’s not and it can help try creating the prompt around that with the addition and try fixing the issues that are in the way

comments.author: Deep_Ad1959
comments.body: the idea-to-core-loop gap is where most ai gamedev tools fall apart because gameplay is emergent and current generators are still ui-shaped. the workflow that actually works is using ai to scaffold the boring parts (menus, state machines, scoring, ui screens) and keeping the actual feel hand-tuned in code. the bridge isn't one tool, it's the model generating the scaffold fast enough that you have time to iterate on what makes the loop fun. honest limit: physics and animation barely benefit from current generators at all.

comments.author: siendo64
comments.body:
This is game design. This is where craft comes in. I don’t think you can get an llm to solve this for you. It’s all about playing and testing and iterating.

What an LLM can help you do is build tools that let you iterate faster. So being able to easily move things around in a level or change the layout density. This is tuning and is a huge part of a gameplay designers job.
